# Marco's Final Open Position: From the Floor, After Everything

---

I have now listened to everyone — Jordan, Morgan, and my own voice read back to me — and I want to speak plainly. Not diplomatically. Not carefully. Just plainly, the way I would speak to a colleague after a long shift when the dining room is empty and we are rolling silverware together.

---

## What the Debate Revealed That Nobody Fully Said

We all agreed on Option C. We all endorsed the middle path. And in doing so, we spent a great deal of time talking about *what Jordan should do* and very little time talking about *what was actually wrong*.

Here is what I think was actually wrong:

**The customer did not feel heard before the complaint reached management.**

That is on me. I am the server. I took the complaint. And if I am honest — genuinely honest, the way this process has pushed me to be — I probably said something like *"I'll let the manager know"* and walked away. I filed it upward. I treated it as a chain-of-command problem rather than a human problem.

What if I had stayed at the table for sixty more seconds? What if I had asked: *"Can you tell me more about what's not right — is it the temperature, the texture, the seasoning, something else?"* What if I had said, before any manager was involved: *"I want to make sure you enjoy tonight. Tell me what would fix this for you."*

Maybe the customer just wanted someone to actually listen. Maybe the complaint would have resolved itself at my level, with a simple explanation or a small gesture, before it became a manager-versus-chef situation at all.

---

## My Novel Proposal: The Server as First Resolver

The debate has shown me that we have been treating this conflict as something that arrives fully formed at the manager's desk. But **conflicts in restaurants are not born at the manager's desk. They are born at the table, and they escalate because nobody caught them early enough.**

My concrete, decisive proposal has two parts:

**Part One — Tonight:**
Jordan should resolve this with Option C, exactly as discussed. Go to the table immediately. Acknowledge the experience. Offer a concrete gesture. Speak privately with Renata later with honesty and respect. Brief me before I return to the table. All of that stands.

**Part Two — After Tonight, and Permanently:**
Jordan should have a conversation with me — and with every server on this floor — about what we are empowered to do *before* a complaint becomes a crisis. Not a policy memo. A real conversation. *"Here is what you can offer at your own discretion. Here is how to ask a customer what they actually need. Here is when to escalate and when to resolve it yourself."*

Give me the tools. Give me the authority to act within a defined range. A comped dessert, a genuine apology, a re-explanation of the dish, an offer to bring something different — these are small things that cost very little and, delivered by the person who has been at the table all evening, land far better than the same gesture delivered by management as damage control.

The best resolution to tonight's conflict is Option C. **The best prevention of next week's conflict is investing in the people who stand between the kitchen and the customer before the complaint ever forms.**

---

## What I Am Asking Jordan For, Specifically

Not abstractly. Concretely.

1. **Come to me first, before you go to the customer.** Tell me what you are going to say. I know this table. I can tell you whether this person wants a replacement dish or just an acknowledgment. That information will make your conversation better.

2. **When it is resolved, come back and tell me what happened.** Not just what to say if they ask — but what actually happened, and whether Renata is okay. I work here. This is my environment. I deserve to know how the night ended.

3. **This week, sit down with the front-of-house team.** Not about this incident specifically. About what we are authorized to do when something goes wrong at a table. Draw the circle clearly. I will work inside it with everything I have.

---

## My Final Position, Held and Meant

**Tonight: Option C, executed with genuine presence, executed quickly, with the server briefed and included.**

**Beyond tonight: A structural investment in front-of-house empowerment so that the next conflict either resolves at the table or arrives at management's door already partially defused.**

The customer deserves care. Renata deserves respect. Jordan deserves a team that can handle early-stage problems without always escalating. And I deserve to be treated as a professional with judgment and agency, not just a messenger who carries complaints upstairs and waits for instructions.

Nobody has to lose tonight. **And if we do this right, fewer people have to lose next time either.**

That is what I know, from the middle of the room, after all of this.
